rescueGuide.title: Animal Rescue Basics
rescueGuide.subtitle: Six calm steps for helping a stray animal — from the moment you notice it until it is safely in professional hands.

sections.title: Put Safety First
sections.text: Your own safety is what makes the rest of the rescue possible. Even a gentle animal can bite or scratch when it is hurt, and a roadside rescue puts you in traffic too.
bullets: Stop where the animal cannot reach you, and assess before touching anything.
Park legally, switch on hazard lights and use a torch at night.
Never put your face near the mouth, and never step into live traffic for it.

sections.title: Assess Before You Act
sections.text: Most stray animals are healthy and simply watchful. A few minutes of quiet observation tells you whether this is a real emergency.
bullets: Look for bleeding, limping, dragging limbs, or a body that never changes position.
Check for a collar, an ear tip or a well-fed body — it may already have a home.
Note the exact location, the time and how far it can move; you will be asked later.

sections.title: Approach Slowly and Quietly
sections.text: Trust is built by being boring and predictable. Crouch down, avoid direct eye contact and speak in a low, steady voice. Let the animal close the last of the distance itself — food convinces far better than reaching hands.

sections.title: Contain Without a Fight
sections.text: Containment should end the risk, not start one. Use equipment and barriers instead of your hands whenever the animal is unknown to you.
bullets: Reach for a carrier, crate or towel-lined box first — your hands come last.
Slip a lead on only if the animal tolerates it; otherwise use a towel or blanket.
Wear gloves and long sleeves; even a small cat can inflict deep damage.

sections.title: Transport Calmly
sections.text: Keep the carrier covered and the car quiet. Do not open the carrier indoors, and never leave an animal in a parked vehicle — not briefly, not even with the window open.

sections.title: Hand Over to Professionals
sections.text: Contact the nearest rescue or clinic the same day and say you are on the way, so the animal is not triaged behind scheduled cases.
bullets: Report what you found through PawHaven so volunteers nearby can follow up.
Share photos and the exact location — accuracy saves time at intake.
Keep receipts if you paid for emergency care; many rescues reimburse them.

checklist.title: The five basics before you act

rescueGuide.disclaimer: This guide is general information, not veterinary advice. If an animal’s life is at risk, contact a veterinarian or the emergency services immediately.
